text.title: Design System Governance Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for the umbrella operating model: who holds decision rights, what mechanically triggers an RFC, how long a proposal may sit before a default outcome fires, and how the artefact references the deprecation and breaking-change policies instead of duplicating their timelines.

rule.statement: `owners` MUST assign exactly one named individual per pillar — tokens/foundations, accessibility, core components, platform adapters, documentation — and every component and token in the system MUST resolve to exactly one pillar. Per-component owner tables and unassigned pillars block approval of the artefact.

rationale.source: Nathan Curtis, 'Team Models for Scaling a Design System' (centralised / federated / hybrid) + RACI

rule.rationale: Per-component ownership tables go stale at the first refactor that splits or merges components, and a contributor whose component is not in the table gets bounced between reviewers until the PR dies. Pillars survive refactors because they are defined by concern, not by file layout.

rule.statement: `contribution_rules` MUST state a mechanical trigger for RFC vs plain PR. Required RFC: a new component, a new token tier or token key, any change classified MAJOR by the breaking-change policy, any change to accessible behaviour or semantics, any new prop on an existing component. Explicitly exempt: bug fixes that restore documented behaviour, documentation, and added visual-regression tests.

rationale.source: Rust RFC process (rust-lang/rfcs, 'substantial change' threshold) and the IETF RFC model

rule.rationale: When the gate is "significant changes need an RFC", the reviewer's judgement decides case by case, so an identical two-line fix is waved through one week and routed to a month-long RFC the next. Contributors who get routed once stop contributing, and the system loses exactly the federated capacity governance exists to organise.

rule.statement: `rfc_pipeline` MUST name every stage with a maximum dwell time and the outcome that fires automatically on expiry — for example: no shepherd assigned within 5 working days → auto-closed with reason; no unresolved objection during a 10-working-day final comment period → accepted, shepherd named. A stage with no expiry default is not a pipeline stage.

rationale.source: Rust RFC 'final comment period' (10 days) and Python PEP 1 resolution states

rule.rationale: Proposals without an expiry default accumulate rather than resolve, because leaving one open is free for everyone involved. A contributor who finds an eight-month-old open RFC for the thing they need builds a local override instead — and that local override is precisely the product-surface fork governance is meant to prevent.

rule.statement: `review_cadence` MUST state a numeric first-response SLA for inbound contribution PRs, and the artefact MUST carry the measured p50 and p90 first-response times for the previous review period. An SLA published without a measurement for the last period is recorded as unmet.

rationale.source: Nathan Curtis, 'Contribution Models for Design Systems'

rule.rationale: An unmeasured SLA cannot fail, so it never triggers the staffing conversation it exists to trigger. Meanwhile the consuming teams do measure it, informally — and once the felt wait exceeds the cost of a local copy, they fork the component and the system's coverage number quietly stops meaning anything.

rule.statement: `deprecation_policy_ref` and `breaking_change_policy_ref` MUST be references to separately versioned documents (URL plus version or commit SHA). The governance artefact MUST NOT inline deprecation window lengths, removal timelines, or the breaking-change classification list — only the reference and the version it was last reconciled against.
rule.rationale: Duplicated timelines diverge along different update paths: the governance doc is edited at onboarding, the policy doc is edited after an incident. The stale copy is the one new teams read, so plans get built against a window that no longer exists, and the mismatch surfaces only when a removal lands earlier than a consumer scheduled for.

rule.statement: `escalation_path` MUST be an ordered chain ending in a single individual with authority to decide within a stated time bound, and MUST state the holding behaviour while escalation is open (default: proposal not merged, existing behaviour unchanged). "The design council decides" with no tie-break holder does not satisfy this rule.

rationale.source: Python PEP 13 steering-council model / consent-based decision rules (sociocracy)

rule.rationale: Consensus-only bodies deadlock on exactly the contested changes that require governance — a token rename whose cost falls on one org unit and whose benefit falls on another. A deadlock has a default outcome whether or not you choose one: the team with the deadline ships a local override, and the decision is made by whoever moved first.

rule.statement: Do NOT apply when the system has one contributor and no consuming team outside that contributor's own repository — the coordination cost exceeds the coordination removed. Also skip when nothing is published or versioned yet; establish a release and a version scheme first. For capture of system implications before a governance model exists, use design-system-impact-queue.

rationale.source: Nathan Curtis, 'Team Models for Scaling a Design System'

rule.rationale: Governance is a mechanism for resolving contention between independent parties. With a single contributor there is no contention to resolve, so the RFC pipeline and escalation chain become paperwork the same person files against themselves and then stops filing.
